layers.name: Core loop and action primitives
layers.question: What can one step express?
layers.evidence: JAZ invoke and RLM recursion; CodeAct; 13 hook events over invoke, LLM query and REPL exec with local and dynamic scope; StuLife far-recall 69.9 vs Letta 61.8 at 43% of the cost; an uncapped run reached depth 70 (JAZ pp. 4-7, 14). A reproduction of RLM reports depth-2 recursion cutting accuracy (secondary).

layers.name: State, context and memory
layers.question: What persists, where, and who can read it?
layers.evidence: Typed boards (Agensh: OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM, PATCH_SUMMARY, capped entries, grep over history), verified gists (DeLM, secondary), ACE playbooks (secondary), history as a first-class variable passed by reference (JAZ); context clash and poisoning are the named failure modes.

layers.name: Topology and coordination
layers.question: Who decides what, and how do agents meet?
layers.evidence: Agensh scales 1 to 1,024 agents without an orchestrator (pandoc 33.89% to 55.06%; means over the five hardest ProgramBench instances); HERMES directed typed messages and single-writer rule; MASS topology as an integer block vector under an agent budget; the agent-scaling study (2512.08296) +80.8% to -70.0% and MAST 37% inter-agent misalignment are secondary.

layers.name: Verification, adjudication and revision
layers.question: How is the final answer chosen and repaired?
layers.evidence: VeriHarness: 34% of unanimous claims wrong, 74% of disagreements hold the right alternative (Opus 4.8 on APEX-Agents, 1,692 claims); claim-check-evidence-verdict records with an unresolved state; HERMES: deterministic failures can never be PASS; HarnessDev: self-reported status is never a scoring input.

layers.name: Optimizing the harness itself
layers.question: What is searched, and by whom?
layers.evidence: MASS block-first optimization (largest stage gain +6); MILO dominance admission with held-out re-scoring but headline numbers include the search split; HarnessDev: 2 clear positives in 64 switches, held-out optimal 2 of 9, fixed-executor regressions to -10.32; the harness-evolution evaluation (2607.12227) +0.6 and AHE 11.6% are secondary.

layers.name: Distillation and co-evolution with weights
layers.question: What moves into weights, and what stays external?
layers.evidence: Harness-Zero: 23.3% to 44.3% macro average for a 9B student under a single-tool harness; per-pattern recovery 40-100%; USPTO trails the source harness; guards survive only as learned behaviour; OPHSD, EvoHarness-RL and WHALE are secondary.

layers.name: Governance, safety and economics
layers.question: What bounds the system?
layers.evidence: JAZ budgets, iteration, recursion and context-window hooks; HERMES revision budget B (default 3, returns beyond 3 at most 0.9 points); HarnessDev 500-step and 7,200 s caps with a liveness guard; VeriHarness read-only workspace and information boundary; SLSA/Sigstore provenance and Anthropic's multiagent findings are secondary.

layers.name: Evaluation and benchmarks
layers.question: What is the unit of evaluation?
layers.evidence: Report (model, harness, budget, agent count); HarnessDev 2,207 instances over five benchmarks with avg@3, a ±4.75-point noise band and executor tokens beside score; MILO k=3 rollouts and task-clustered CIs; VeriHarness three verifier seeds and judge-drift control; JAZ distinct cache key per run; Harness-Bench is secondary.

principles.principle: Minimal primitives, maximal expressivity: delegation, memory and self-improvement are programs over one recursive primitive
principles.counterEvidence: depth-2 overthinking; unstructured flexibility breeds specification failures

principles.principle: Separate harness from model, but measure the pairing
principles.counterEvidence: evolved harnesses transfer weakly across models

principles.principle: Evidence over consensus; investigate in separate contexts; adjudicate fresh

principles.counterEvidence: Agensh still gains to 1,024 agents on decomposable work

principles.principle: For wide, decomposable work, self-organize over shared infrastructure rather than route through one main agent
Verify before admitting to shared state
Search the whole harness and the search strategy; keep negative evidence and full traces
Evolve on development tasks, gate on held-out, compare to matched-budget sampling, red-team for shortcuts
Distill procedural behaviour; keep knowledge-heavy or volatile capability external
Govern through hooks and budgets, not prompts
principles.counterEvidence: hooks do not solve incentive conflicts

principles.principle: Design for caching and incremental contexts

critique.figure: Harness evolution gains only +0.6 points on held-out tasks and does not consistently beat matched-budget parallel sampling (2607.12227, as reported by RS-CLAUDE).
critique.consequence: Evolution waits behind the admission gate (MAS-RA-005): held-out split, matched-budget baseline.

critique.figure: AHE's per-edit regression predictions: 5 of 43 predicted regressions materialized, a precision of 11.6% (as reported by RS-CLAUDE).
critique.consequence: An agent's own regression forecast is not admission evidence; keep negative evidence and full traces (P8).

critique.figure: HarnessDev: feedback-pair gains of +3.0 to +13.9 shrink to +1.43 to +4.44 on the held-out 630; under the fixed Gemini executor only one of four lineages (Opus, +2.70) improves held-out and the other three regress, down to -10.32; of 64 version switches only 2 are clear positives (pp. 1, 11-13).

papers.title: Harness Engineering for Software Engineering via Modular Executable Dev-Primitives (HERMES)
papers.status: arXiv 2610.07832v1 [cs.SE], 6 Oct 2026; preprint; no venue named in the 30 pages.
papers.codeAvailability: NOT_FOUND. No code, data, artifact URL, DOI or licence statement in the paper (all 30 pages checked). Header 'Preprint.'; results come from the authors' unreleased implementation (p.26). Only prompts (pp.16-20), Algorithm 1 (p.21) and serving details (Qwen3-8B via Ollama on NVIDIA A40, p.21) are disclosed.

claims.claim: Dev-Primitives: repository artefacts (source, config, test files) each own a resident LLM; they pass constraints peer-to-peer along dependency edges.
claims.finding: Sec 3.2 p.4: a Dev-Primitive wraps an individual repository component (source, configuration or test file; F.5 p.24 adds build specs, scripts, service definitions) with a resident LLM. Messages are 'directed rather than broadcast' (p.4), sent only to the callers, callees, configurations and tests the primitive's local reasoning implicates, so topology follows the repository's dependency structure (p.3 Key Differences, p.4). Qualifications the synthesis omits: (a) only the activated subset P_A = {P_i | i in A} is ever instantiated, not every artefact (p.4; eq.3 p.14); (b) the dependency edges are inferred by the model reading candidate files, not taken from a precomputed call graph (F.1 p.21); (c) 'model hidden states are not preserved across calls' (F.5 p.24), i.e. 'resident' means a per-call LLM bound to the artifact plus persisted artifact-and-message state, not a long-lived process; (d) delivery is mediated by the harness, which places each message verbatim into the target's context with no central rewriting (F.5 p.24).

claims.claim: A dynamic activation mechanism wakes only task-relevant primitives by following dependencies.
claims.finding: p.2 and Sec 3.3 p.4: activation localizes the components likely to implement the reported behavior, follows their dependencies to callers, configurations and tests, and instantiates only that candidate set. Formal: Pi = ACTIVATE(q, R) = {(i, x_i)}_{i in A}, P_A = {P_i | i in A} (eq.2-3 p.14). Five operations: issue analysis, component localization, dependency analysis, task decomposition, edit planning (B.1 p.14). Implemented as 'a single LLM call chain' that inspects repository structure and reads candidate files; explicitly not a static retriever (F.1 p.21). Prompt principle: activate only primitives required for the current iteration (C.1 p.16). Observed size: 4.7 (SWE-bench Verified), 12.6 (SWE Refactor Bench), 6.8 (Terminal-Bench 4.0), 5.4 (DevOps-Gym) distinct primitives per task (Table 8 p.9).

claims.claim: Execution evidence (test or run failures) is diagnosed back to implicated primitives, which are reactivated for targeted repair.
claims.finding: p.5 and B.4 p.15: v = DIAGNOSE(q, Pi, R', o) in {PASS, FAIL}; on FAIL, structured feedback phi = (e, c, u) = observed failure, suspected root cause with the components implicated by the evidence, revision guidance; 'the component set named in c is what keeps revision localized' (p.5). Replan Pi' = ACTIVATE(q, R', Pi, phi) may retune objectives, drop components or activate newly implicated ones until PASS or budget B is exhausted (p.5; eq.8 p.15; Algorithm 1 p.21). Qualification: diagnosis does not reactivate primitives itself; its output 'is returned to the activation module', which performs the selective reactivation (p.15). Evidence vector o = (o_shell, o_test, o_runtime, o_trace) (eq.6 p.15).

claims.claim: Average improvement of 12.4 percentage points over matched harness baselines.
claims.finding: Abstract p.1 prints '12.4%'; intro p.2 and conclusion p.10 print '12.4 percentage points on average'. SCOPE the synthesis should carry: the figure is the default GPT-5.6 Sol, medium reasoning effort, B = 3 configuration averaged over the four benchmarks (p.2), not an average over all backbones. Reconstruction from the tables: SWE-bench Verified +0.80 vs mini-SWE-agent (Table 1 p.5), SWE Refactor Bench +24.5 vs Codex (Table 2 p.6), Terminal-Bench 4.0 +18.8 vs Codex (Table 3 p.7), DevOps-Gym +5.52 vs Codex (Table 4 p.7); mean = 12.405. Benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified (500 instances), SWE Refactor Bench (20 whole-repository migration tasks), Terminal-Bench 4.0 (66 tasks, 5 trials each), DevOps-Gym (build/configuration, monitoring, issue resolving, test generation). Seven primary backbones (p.5): GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Terra, GPT-5.6 Luna (OpenAI); Claude Sonnet 5, Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic); DeepSeek-V4; Qwen3-8B. Table 10 p.22 lists further backbones used in individual tables: GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4 Mini, GPT-5 Mini, GPT-5.3-Codex, o4-mini, Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8/4.7/4.6/4.5, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Claude Sonnet 4, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Pro Preview, Gemini 3 Pro, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.7 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek-V3.1, Qwen3-Coder-30B, Qwen3.8-Max, Kimi-K3, GLM-5.2, GLM-5.3, Grok 4.6, Grok 4.5. Baseline harnesses: mini-SWE-agent, Claude Code, Codex (SWE-bench, Refactor, Terminal-Bench), Grok Build (Terminal-Bench), OpenHands, SageAgent, Aider (DevOps-Gym). Per-backbone gains range from 0.00 (Claude Opus 5, SWE-bench) to +31.70 (Claude Sonnet 4 vs Aider, DevOps-Gym).

claims.claim: Heterogeneous allocation: Qwen3-8B primitives come within 4.5% of a homogeneous GPT-5.6 configuration at 26.2% less cost.
claims.finding: Three corrections of precision. (a) Unit: the gap is 4.5 percentage points, not 4.5% relative. The abstract p.1 prints 'within 4.5%' but p.2 and p.10 print '4.5 percentage points'; it is the worst case across the four benchmarks, on SWE Refactor Bench (26.5 vs 31.0 composite, Table 6 p.8); the other gaps are 2.8 (SWE-bench Verified 94.2 vs 97.0), 1.2 (Terminal-Bench 4.0 50.6 vs 51.8) and 3.11 (DevOps-Gym 52.30 vs 55.41). (b) Model name: the comparison is against 'homogeneous GPT-5.6 Sol' (GPT-5.6 Sol for activation, Dev-Primitives and diagnosis); the heterogeneous configuration is GPT-5.6 Sol activation / Qwen3-8B Dev-Primitives / GPT-5.6 Sol diagnosis, i.e. strong models still run activation and diagnosis. (c) Scope of the cost figure: the 26.2% reduction is measured only on Terminal-Bench 4.0, $2.51k vs $3.40k total inference cost (Table 7 p.8; (3.40-2.51)/3.40 = 26.2%), not across all benchmarks. Related printed figure: with GPT-5.5 diagnosis instead, 49.7% at $2.13k, '37.4% lower total inference cost', 2.1 points below homogeneous (p.8).

claims.claim: Code or data availability and a licence statement.
claims.finding: No code repository URL, data release, artifact DOI, reproducibility checklist or licence statement appears on any of the 30 pages. The only implementation disclosures are the prompt templates (Appendix C pp.16-20), Algorithm 1 (p.21), backbone serving details (Qwen3-8B via Ollama on NVIDIA A40, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, 32K context; all other models via official APIs; p.21 and pp.29-30) and baseline provenance (F.8 pp.25-26). The authors state 'All HERMES results are obtained with our implementation' (p.26) without releasing it.

facts: Activation plan is an auditable JSON: per component objective, dependencies, communication_targets, expected_action in {inspect, modify, validate}; no numeric cap on activations (observed 4.7-12.6 per task) (pp. 16-17, 9).
Messages are directed, typed {interface, dependency, behavior, test, configuration} with required_action, delivered verbatim; single-writer rule per artifact (pp. 18-19, 24).

Diagnosis returns PASS/FAIL plus failure_evidence, suspected_causes, missing_components, revision_guidance; failing visible tests or compile errors can never be PASS on model judgment (pp. 15, 20-21).
The 12.4-point headline is the GPT-5.6 Sol, medium-effort, B=3 average over four benchmarks; Claude Opus 5 gains 0.00 on SWE-bench Verified (pp. 2, 5-7).
Correction: the heterogeneous gap is 4.5 percentage points worst case and the 26.2% cost cut is Terminal-Bench 4.0 only; strong models still run activation and diagnosis (p. 8).
Known weakness: PASS issued on a green regression run after every reproducer failed to build; no code, data or licence released (pp. 29, 26).
contractImplications: Activation output must be an explicit, auditable plan: per-component objective, dependencies, communication_targets and expected_action in {inspect, modify, validate}; a primitive may be activated to inspect and send messages without ever editing its file (p.17, p.28).
Dependency expansion in the paper is LLM-driven with no static call graph; a contract should record which mechanism produced each edge and not assume a precomputed graph (p.21, p.14).

No numeric cap on activated components, files read or tokens is specified by the paper; any limit a contract imposes is the contract's own, calibrated against the observed 4.7-12.6 activations per task (p.9, p.16).

Messages are directed (one source, one target), typed in {interface, dependency, behavior, test, configuration}, carry a required_action, and are delivered verbatim with no central rewriting or filtering (p.19, p.24).

Single-writer rule per artifact: a primitive may modify only its own file and must route every cross-file requirement through a message, including 'I lack the information, you own this dependency' (p.18).
Round semantics: messages emitted in a round must reach their targets before the round closes, and a target may re-run its local modification in the same round (p.4, p.15, p.24).

Diagnosis is a verdict plus structured feedback (failure_evidence by source, suspected_causes by component, missing_components, revision_guidance by component); it never edits and only the activation module acts on it (p.15, p.20).
Deterministic failures are non-negotiable: failing task-visible tests, failed compilation or observed runtime failures cannot be marked PASS on model judgment (p.15, p.21, p.22).

Revision budget semantics: B counts rounds after the initial plan-modify-execute-diagnose pass, B=0 still runs one full pass, default B=3, and returns beyond 3 are at most 0.9 points (p.16, p.21, p.23).

Evaluation isolation: held-out tests and graders must be invisible during solving; FAIL_TO_PASS and PASS_TO_PASS run only after termination; self-built reproducers and repository tests are permitted inside (p.22, p.25).

A PASS with only a green regression run and no failing-to-passing reproducer is weak evidence; a contract that wants certification should require a task-specific reproducer or label such passes as consistency-only (p.29).

Primitive state is the artifact version plus accumulated messages; no model hidden state survives a call, so every reactivation must be fully reconstructible from stored artifact, objective and context (p.24).
Files created during solving must be registered as primitives for later rounds; transient outputs, caches and logs are environment observations, not components (p.24).
Cost accounting must include all activation, primitive and diagnosis calls over the full trajectory, and must distinguish distinct activated components from repeated primitive calls (p.26, p.27).
Heterogeneous allocation is the Pareto choice: strong models for activation and diagnosis, cheap models for primitives; diagnosis strength matters more than activation strength (p.8, Table 6 and 7).

Selection quality should be reported as recall and precision against a reference component set, micro-averaged, union over all rounds, and interpreted as agreement with one repair path rather than ground truth (p.23, p.29).

Expect per-task latency to rise by roughly 10-270% over single-agent harnesses on SWE-bench depending on backbone (GPT-5.6 Sol 182.37 -> 205.34 s; GPT-5.5 under Codex 108.54 -> 398.74 s), except where baselines were already slow (Claude Sonnet 5 962.37 -> 824.63 s) (Table 1 p.5); a contract SLA must budget for this.

Disabling on-demand activation keeps the same component set but raises cost 1.61-1.88x and loses up to 3.0 points, so deactivation between rounds is a cost control, not just a quality one (p.27, p.9).

papers.title: VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks
papers.status: arXiv 2610.00972v1 [cs.AI], 1 Oct 2026; no peer-reviewed venue stated; code and dataset links in Appendix E (p.22).
papers.codeAvailability: Verification code: https://github.com/google-research/veriharness. Rollout pools: a Hugging Face dataset linked on p.22 (trajectory, delivered files and grader score per rollout; no benchmark inputs, rubrics or reference answers; official task IDs included; about 26,000 rollouts over five benchmarks and two models). Website: veriharness.com. Licence: not stated in the paper for either release; the runtime builds on the pi coding agent (MIT license) and serves Claude via a local LiteLLM proxy (p.21-22). Links were not fetched (no network used).

claims.claim: The same base model used for generation acts as an agentic verifier with a workspace, evidence tools and reusable verification skills.
claims.finding: Abstract (p.1): the harness turns the generator's own LLM into an agentic verifier by giving it a workspace, evidence tools, and reusable verification skills. Formalised p.5 Eq. (2): Verifier = (M, H_V), H_V = (W, T, Pi, S) = workspace, evidence tools, verification protocol, skill library (Table 5, p.23). The verifier uses the same model AND the same tools as the generator (p.3) and has no access to the grader, reference answers or rubrics (p.3, p.7, p.21).

claims.claim: Two components: a disagreement resolver (tests competing claims against environmental evidence; expected information gain) and a consensus challenger (searches for omitted requirements or flawed logic in unanimous claims); separate contexts; fresh-context adjudication.
claims.finding: Resolver (Sec. 3.2, p.5): locates a disputed claim p and its candidate values V_p, traces them to sources/computations, prefers the check with the largest expected information gain Gain(chi) = E[H(b_p) - H(b_p(.|E(chi))) | e_<k] (Eq. 3), eliminates contradicted candidates V_p <- {v consistent with e} (Eq. 4), records outcomes in L_neq. Challenger (Sec. 3.3, p.5-6): identifies consensus claims, proposes how each could fail, tests those possibilities against the environment, prioritises by Priority(chi) = P(chi exposes a failure of the consensus claim | t, R, e_<k) (Eq. 5); three kinds: consensus values (recompute from raw inputs, compare labels with source metadata), consensus readings (interpretation vs the named file, period, definition), consensus omissions (requirements every rollout overlooked); records in L_eq. Separate contexts: Sec. 3.4 p.6 ('so that disputed claims do not displace attention from consensus claims'); p.21: both run concurrently and 'neither reads the other's record'; Algorithm 1 line 2, p.20. Adjudication: a fresh context of the same model reviews both records with the task and rollouts without inheriting either investigator's history (p.6, Eq. 6; Algorithm 1 line 11).

claims.claim: 34% of unanimous claims were wrong; 74% of disagreements contained the right alternative.
claims.finding: Figure 2 (p.2) and Sec. 2 (p.4): consensus claims (H=0, n=917) 66% correct / 34% wrong; disputed claims (H>0, n=775) 74% contain a correct candidate, and the most frequent answer is correct in only 47%. Scope (Appendix A, p.19): offline analysis of ten-rollout pools of Claude Opus 4.8 on APEX-Agents only, 434 tasks, 1,692 claims; one rubric criterion = one claim; values extracted by Claude Opus 4.8 at temperature zero; correctness from the benchmark's own per-criterion grades. Not a cross-benchmark or cross-model statistic.

claims.claim: Revision gains over a single rollout of +6.2 and +6.4 points with two frontier models.
claims.finding: Abstract p.1 and Table 2 p.8: with evidence-backed revision, the 'Avg' column (unweighted mean over the five benchmarks, three-seed mean) rises from 47.2 to 53.4 (+6.2) with 'Gemini 3.5 Flash' and from 49.6 to 56.1 (+6.4) with 'Claude Opus 4.8'. These are five-benchmark averages, not one benchmark. Benchmarks as printed: 'APEX-Agents (v1.0)', 'Workspace-Bench Lite' (WSB), 'WorkBuddy Bench', 'SpreadsheetBench 2' (SB-2), 'JobBench'. Per-benchmark revision gains, Flash: +6.7 APEX, +8.9 WSB, +5.0 WorkBuddy, +4.9 SB-2, +5.3 JobBench; Opus: +11.7 APEX, +6.8 WSB, +4.7 WorkBuddy, +4.2 SB-2, +4.8 JobBench. Selection-only gains are smaller: +4.4 (Flash, 51.6) and +4.1 (Opus, 53.7). Figure 1 (p.1) headlines Flash-with-revision gains of 6.7 on APEX-Agents and 8.9 on WSB.

claims.claim: 86-91% prompt-cache hit rate from incremental contexts.
claims.finding: Appendix K (p.27): because the harness's calls are incremental turns over one workspace, 86 to 91% of its input tokens are served from cache. Stated as the share of input tokens served from cache (token share, not a per-request hit rate). If cached tokens were charged at the full input price, selection would cost $5.40 (Flash) and $13.06 (Opus) per task and still sit on the frontier because baselines re-read whole rollouts on every call.

claims.claim: It beats an LLM-as-a-Verifier baseline.
claims.finding: Table 2 (p.8), five-benchmark Avg, three-seed means. Gemini 3.5 Flash: LLM-as-a-Verifier 49.5 vs VeriHarness (select) 51.6 vs VeriHarness with revision 53.4. Per benchmark (LLM-as-a-Verifier / VeriHarness select / VeriHarness): APEX 49.8 / 53.3 / 54.8; WSB 60.4 / 62.0 / 65.4; WorkBuddy 75.3 / 77.8 / 78.2; SB-2 30.2 / 31.5 / 32.2; JobBench 31.9 / 33.5 / 36.2. Claude Opus 4.8: LLM-as-a-Verifier 51.2 vs VeriHarness (select) 53.7 vs VeriHarness 56.1. Per benchmark: APEX 36.7 / 41.2 / 47.5; WSB 62.4 / 65.0 / 67.3; WorkBuddy 81.7 / 83.0 / 83.7; SB-2 30.2 / 33.4 / 34.3; JobBench 45.0 / 46.1 / 47.6. Figure 1 (p.1) labels LLM-as-a-Verifier 'prior best' for Flash. Cost (Appendix K p.27): Flash selection $1.44/task, a tenth of LLM-as-a-Verifier's cost at twice the gain; Opus selection $3.92/task, about half its cost. Baseline = LLM-as-a-Verifier (arXiv 2607.05391), which decomposes the task into criteria and ranks candidates by per-criterion pairwise comparisons (p.21), run with four evaluations per comparison (p.27).

claims.claim: Skills named evidence, resolve, falsify and repair, and skill evolution from failure feedback.
claims.finding: Appendix H, Table 6 (p.25): eighteen human-authored skills of four kinds with file prefixes evidence-, resolve-, falsify-, repair-. Six evidence skills (evidence-xlsx, -pdf, -docx, -pptx, -bundle, -patch) that render a deliverable as evidence rather than extracted text and ship scripts (xlsx_dump, xlsx_diff, xlsx_gaps, xlsx_forks, xlsx_render, pdf_render, pdf_tables, pdf_words, docx_changes, docx_text, pptx_render, pptx_text, bundle_inventory, patchlab, pageprobe). Four resolver skills (resolve-answer, -bundle, -workbook, -patch): what counts as deciding evidence and the order of authority. Three challenger skills (falsify-answer, -bundle, -workbook): ways a whole pool goes wrong together, one check per entry. Five revision skills (repair-prose, -bundle, -record, -xlsx with xlsx_recalc, -patch): how the type is graded, how an unresolved claim is closed, what must never be edited. Prose kind names are evidence / resolver / challenger / revision (p.24). Definition (p.5): a skill is a reusable failure mode plus its checking procedure in a short text with an optional script; skills exclude task-specific answers. Skill evolution (Sec. 5 p.9; Appendix I p.26): Claude Opus 4.8 reads development-failure packages (task, workspace, rollouts, evidence records, revision plan, delivered artifact, grader per-item verdicts) and proposes K=3 then K=5 candidate libraries per round; a candidate with the largest nonnegative paired development gain replaces the library; an automatic filter rejects candidates containing task identifiers, benchmark names, development filenames or reference-answer values; scripts limited to ten minutes; 10 rounds (C) / 8 rounds (D). Held-out scores (Figure 4 p.9): APEX-Agents A empty 38.6, B human 45.3, C evolved-from-empty 49.6, D evolved-from-human 52.1; SpreadsheetBench 2: 32.8 / 35.7 / 38.5 / 39.4; D adds 6.8 (APEX) and 3.7 (SB-2) over B. Of the 95 evolved checks, 5 restate a human check, 48 make one concrete, 42 are new (p.10).

claims.claim: Adjudicator outputs: a base response, an evidence-backed revision plan, unresolved claims.
claims.finding: Sec. 3.4 Eq. (6), p.6: (base, revision_plan, unresolved) = A(L_neq, L_eq, t, R). base is a rollout in R or the empty set (no usable starting point); revision_plan specifies the changes to make and their supporting evidence; unresolved lists claims the evidence has not settled. Base selection rule: the rollout with the fewest evidence-supported defects on the task's substantive requirements, weighting findings by their importance to the deliverable. Adjudication can uphold, overturn, or leave findings unresolved. Delivery (Eq. 7): r* = Apply(base, revision_plan, unresolved); verification record C = (L_neq, L_eq, base, revision_plan, unresolved). Algorithm 1 lines 11-15 (p.20).

claims.claim: A released rollout corpus and code; a licence statement.
claims.statusDetail: VERIFIED for the code and the rollout corpus; NOT_FOUND for a licence (pp. 1, 22).
claims.finding: p.1: the authors release 'the full pool of approximately 26,000 rollouts' across all five benchmarks and both models, produced at a cost of over $100,000. Appendix E (p.22): rollout pools at a Hugging Face dataset linked on p.22 and verification code at github.com/google-research/veriharness; each rollout contains the trajectory, the delivered files and the benchmark grader's score; no benchmark content is redistributed (no task descriptions, input workspaces, rubrics, reference answers); every rollout carries the official task identifier; pool-only results (single-rollout and selection-oracle rows, Figure 6 curves) are reproducible without running a model.

facts: Claim = (requirement p, per-rollout value v); omission is an explicit value 'absent'; consensus (H=0) and disputed (H>0) claims route to different checkers (pp. 3-4).

Every evidence-record entry links claim, check, evidence, verdict; verdict states are supported, contradicted, new value established by evidence, unresolved; no scalar rollout score by design (pp. 3, 5-6, 12).
Resolver and challenger run in separate contexts that cannot read each other; adjudication in a fresh context; merging contexts costs 0.8 points (pp. 6, 10, 21).
Scope of the 34%/74% figures: Claude Opus 4.8 on APEX-Agents only, 434 tasks, 1,692 claims (p. 19); +6.2/+6.4 are five-benchmark averages with revision; selection-only +4.4/+4.1 (p. 8).
Workspace: rollouts, inputs and environment read-only, one writable output dir, no network; verifier never sees grader, rubric or reference answers (pp. 3, 7, 21).
70% of surviving unanimous errors were checked at an upstream intermediate rather than the graded quantity; a recomputation matching the pool is not confirmation (pp. 10, 27).
86-91% is the share of input tokens served from cache, not a hit rate; revision costs about 3x selection (p. 27). Code and a 26,000-rollout corpus released; licence not stated in the paper (p. 22).
contractImplications: Claim = (requirement/question p, per-rollout value v_{i,p}); equivalent expressions collapse to one value and omission is a distinct value 'absent', so a contract must represent absence explicitly (p.3, p.19).

Partition claims by pool entropy: H=0 consensus vs H>0 disputed, and route them to different checkers; the two populations have different error modes (34% wrong vs 74% correct-candidate-available) (p.2, p.4).
Every evidence-record entry must link claim -> check -> evidence -> verdict, so revisions are traceable and open issues preserved (p.6).
Verdict states needed: supported, contradicted, new value established by evidence, unresolved/open; a new value may be recorded only when evidence establishes it (p.3, p.5).
No scalar rollout score is produced; the contract is per-claim, and any rollout-level score would be a separate, future calibration layer (p.12).

Unresolved claims must stay marked unsettled in the delivered record; multi-slot formats present both readings with the base's first, single-slot formats take the adjudicator's preferred reading (p.6, p.20).
Adjudication output tuple is (base in R or empty, revision_plan with supporting evidence per change, unresolved list); base = empty triggers rebuild from inputs and evidence (p.6, p.20).
Base-selection rule: fewest evidence-supported defects on the task's substantive requirements, weighted by importance, not majority or judge preference (p.6).
Resolver and challenger must run in separate contexts that cannot read each other's record, with adjudication in a fresh context; merging contexts costs 0.8 points on average (p.6, p.10, p.21-22).
Workspace rules: rollouts, inputs and environment read-only; one writable output directory; no network; write/edit tools restricted to the output directory (p.21, p.24).
Information boundary: the verifier never sees grader, rubric or reference answers; skills must not contain task-specific answers (p.3, p.5, p.7, p.21).
Skill schema: a reusable failure mode plus checking procedure, short text with optional script, typed by deliverable (evidence / resolve / falsify / repair) (p.5, p.24-25).
Evidence must come from rendering the deliverable (cell-level spreadsheet text, rendered pages, built and tested patches), not from extracted text (p.21, p.24-25).
Checks should target the graded/delivered quantity, not an upstream intermediate: 70% of surviving shared errors were checked at an input or intermediate quantity (p.10, p.27).
A recomputation that merely matches the pool is not confirmation; the challenger must test an independent property (p.10-11).

Revision guards: empty plan leaves the base unchanged; repair skills define what must never be edited; patches must apply, reproduce and pass what the base passed; xlsx edits need recalculation proof that only targets changed (p.6, p.20, p.25).

Cost accounting fields: per-task cost at list price with cached input at cache-read rate, cache share of input tokens (86-91%), selection cost and revision cost (about 3x selection) reported separately, gain vs single rollout (p.27).
Evaluation contract: three independent verifier runs, cross-seed std, judge-drift control by scoring base and delivered artifacts in the same grading round (p.21).

Skill-evolution boundary: filter task identifiers, benchmark names, development filenames and reference values out of candidate skills; never feed held-out grades back to the proposer; cap script runtime (p.26).

Selection gains are near zero on unanimous pools (+0.6), so any budget policy should spend verification effort on disputed claims and spend consensus-challenging effort only where skills supply prior knowledge (p.10).

papers.title: MILO: Automated Harness Discovery via Orchestrated Multi-Agent Evolution
papers.codeAvailability: Not stated. No repository URL, release statement or licence appears in the text; the title page has a 'Project Page' link button whose URL is not printed (p.1). What is in the paper: prompts reproduced verbatim from the implementation (App. C, p.32-34), full source of the three seed harnesses (Listings 3-5, p.27-31), the minimal harness (Listing 1, p.24), the base DeepAgents harness (Listing 2, p.25-26), the best evolved harness (Listing 14, p.48-52) and optimizer excerpts (Listings 15-18, p.53-55). Baseline code pins: OpenEvolve v0.3.2, ShinkaEvolve v0.0.7, GEPA v0.1.1, EvoX commit 4734f32, A-Evolve commit c9d4789, Meta-Harness commit 44b9942 (p.23). Harnesses are built on the DeepAgents framework and run unchanged against any LangChain chat model or a vLLM server (p.21).

claims.claim: Parallel evolutionary islands with hierarchical lineage memory that keeps rejected mutations as negative evidence.
claims.finding: Abstract: hierarchical lineage memory of island-based trees that uses rejected mutations as negative evidence (p.1). Sec. 4.1.1: memory is append-only and keeps both admitted and rejected children with verdict Adm(h) (p.7). Algorithm 1 line 6 runs all islands 'in parallel' (p.9). Islands 'never compete' (p.3). Table 3(b) caption: rejected grafts persist as negative examples (p.13). K=3 islands in experiments (p.22).

claims.claim: A pool of specialised mutator agents; a meta-orchestrator that can graft mechanisms between islands, speciate crowded-out minority solutions, reassign mutators, and reshape the evaluation curriculum toward high-regret tasks when search stalls.
claims.finding: Sec. 4.1.2: pool G of mutators, off-the-shelf frontier coding agents plus custom agents pairing a frontier LLM with an open-source harness; 'different mutation tendencies' per model-harness pairing (p.8). Nuance: the pool is heterogeneous (6 coding agents differing by model x harness, p.22), not role-specialised. Sec. 4.1.3: orchestrator diagnoses one of four stalls (dry mutator, exhausted lineage, crowded-out niche, whole-population plateau) and applies at most two of REASSIGN(j, mu), GRAFT(j_donor -> j_dst), SPECIATE(h, mu), CURRICULUM(B') which replaces the search set favoring high-regret tasks; regret rho(tau) = max_h Acc - mean_h Acc over admitted harnesses (p.8). Trigger: island stall counter reaches patience P=3 rounds without held-out gain (p.9-10, p.22). Orchestrator is a Claude Code agent with Opus 4.8 (p.22).

claims.claim: Multi-objective evaluation on accuracy, token use and latency.
claims.finding: Sec. 1 key insight (iv): a candidate is admitted only if it advances the Pareto frontier in accuracy, tokens and latency (p.3). Sec. 4.2: fitness vector F(h) in [0,1]^(1+q) with F0 = Acc(h, B_search) and economy 1 - Cost_i/c_i per cost axis (p.9). Cost axes in practice: output tokens and agent seconds, normalized by per-task caps of 20M tokens and 7,200 s (p.22). Nuance: dominance is 'pass-primary' with tolerance eps=0.02, so cost axes decide only when accuracies are within 0.02 (p.22).

claims.claim: Terminal-Bench 2.1 result 86.1% versus a leaderboard top of 83.8%, with 26% fewer tokens than the seed harness.
claims.finding: Abstract: 86.1+-2.0% vs official leaderboard top entry 83.8+-2.3%, consuming 26% fewer tokens than its initial harness (p.1). Table 2(a): MILO RR@5 = 86.1 +-2.0 with Opus 4.8 (p.12). Sec. 5.4: TB2.1 harness uses 0.74x the tokens of Best-of-3 while gaining +12.0 RR@5 (p.12, Tab. 2d). Nuances: metric is resolution rate at k=5 (RR@5); 'seed harness' means Best-of-3, the strongest of three seeds (B12, RR@5 74.1, p.11, p.27); the 83.8 figure appears only in the abstract; the two 95% CIs overlap.

claims.claim: Improvements of 12.0, 28.3 and 10.3 points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, PaperBench and DeepSWE with a model named 'Opus 4.8'; outperforms eight state-of-the-art systems.
claims.finding: Abstract: 'With Opus 4.8, it improves resolution rate over its initial harness by +12.0%, +28.3% and +10.3%' vs best prior search gains +4.5% (GEPA), +18.3% (Meta-Harness) and 0% (p.1); repeated in Sec. 5.4 as RR@k over Best-of-3 (p.11). Table 2(a): TB2.1 RR@5 74.1 -> 86.1; PaperBench RR@3 26.7 -> 55.0; DeepSWE RR@3 59.0 -> 69.3 (p.12). Gains are absolute points vs Best-of-3 (initial harness), not vs the SoTA harnesses. 'eight state-of-the-art harnesses and six search methods' (p.1); the eight: Cline, DeepAgents, Goose, Mini-SWE-Agent, OpenCode, OpenHands, Qwen-Code, Terminus-2; the six: OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, EvoX, A-Evolve, GEPA, Meta-Harness (p.11). Model names exactly as printed: backbones 'Opus 4.8' (closed-source) and 'gpt-oss-120b' (open-weight); mutator pool 'Claude Code ... with Opus 4.8', 'Codex ... with GPT-5.5', DeepAgents with 'Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, gpt-oss-120b, or Qwen3-Coder-480B'; orchestrator 'Opus 4.8'; PaperBench judge 'GPT-5.5'; EinsteinArena backbone 'Opus 5'; ShinkaEvolve baseline bandit arms 'Opus 4.8, GPT-5.5, GPT-5.4, and Sonnet 4.5'; all served via Amazon Bedrock (p.11, p.13, p.21-23, p.52). With gpt-oss-120b the gains are PR@k +11.8, +8.6, +14.8 (p.11, Tab. 3).

claims.claim: An EinsteinArena result: Erdos minimum-overlap problem to 0.3808568.
claims.finding: Abstract: Erdos minimum-overlap 0.3808586 -> 0.3808568 (p.1). Table 5: MILO 0.3808568 vs prior best 0.3808586, TTT-Discover 0.3808753, AlphaEvolve 0.380924 (p.14). Table 9 full precision: 0.3808567744 vs 0.3808585749, margin 1.8e-6, arena minimum improvement 1e-7, rescored by the arena's verifier fetched 2026-09-09 and 2026-09-22 (p.52). Listing 15 header: prior best 0.3808586 -> ours 0.3808568 (p.53). Nuances: obtained with the instance-level variant of MILO (Sec. 4.3) and backbone 'Opus 5', not Opus 4.8 (p.13, p.52); also first autocorrelation 1.50274365 -> 1.50274360 and third 1.4508066 -> 1.4488860 (p.14).

claims.claim: Code availability and licence.
claims.finding: No code-release statement, repository URL or licence appears in the text. The title page shows a 'Project Page' link button whose URL is not printed (p.1). App. A.1 'Reproducibility and Implementation Details' covers hardware, model access and configuration only (p.21-22). Prompts are stated to be reproduced verbatim from the implementation (App. C, p.32) and full source of the seed harnesses (Listings 3-5, p.27-31) and the best evolved harness (Listing 14, p.48-52) is printed. Baseline code pins are given (OpenEvolve v0.3.2, ShinkaEvolve v0.0.7, GEPA v0.1.1, EvoX 4734f32, A-Evolve c9d4789, Meta-Harness 44b9942, p.23); Self-Harness, DarwinX and AIDE2 were skipped because their code is not public (p.11).

facts: Admission: a child is admitted only if no harness in the island's admitted set dominates it; accuracy primary with a 0.02 band, cost axes decide inside the band; no statistical test (pp. 9-10, 22).
Rejected children stay in the append-only lineage with verdict, patch and accuracy/cost deltas as negative evidence (p. 7).
k=3 rollouts per task on a search split for admission; admitted candidates re-scored on a held-out split; stall counter resets only on held-out gain; orchestrator after P=3 rounds (pp. 9-10, 22).
Headline re-evaluations include the search split; the only disjoint test is Frontier-Bench (+3.8 RR@3 over Best-of-3); cross-executor transfer is not measured (pp. 12, 14, 22).
Gains +12.0/+28.3/+10.3 are against the Best-of-3 seed, not the eight SoTA harnesses; 86.1±2.0 vs 83.8±2.3 has overlapping CIs (pp. 1, 11-12).
Search cost: 72 h wall-clock cap, 45-min mutation calls, K=3 islands; total tokens and dollars unreported; no code or licence, full harness sources printed (pp. 21-23, 27-52).
contractImplications: Admit a candidate only if no already-admitted harness on its lineage dominates it (positive hypervolume contribution), not merely if it beats its parent (Eq. 7, p.10).
Make accuracy primary with a +-0.02 tolerance band: a >0.02 accuracy drop is rejected regardless of cost savings, and cost axes decide only inside the band (p.22).
Score candidates with k=3 rollouts per task on a search split before admission; re-evaluate at leaderboard k only for the final pick (p.22).
Keep a disjoint held-out split; stall counters and the final selection key on held-out gain, never on search-split gain alone (Algorithm 1 lines 12-13 and 22, p.9; p.10).
Report headline numbers on tasks disjoint from the search split; MILO's own clean test is Frontier-Bench (+3.8 RR@3, Table 4 p.14) while its headline re-evaluation includes search tasks (p.12, p.22).
Record rejected candidates with verdict, patch and deltas; they are negative evidence that later mutators must not retry (Eq. 3, p.7; Listing 14, p.48).
Per-candidate record: accuracy, normalized cost vector, per-rollout traces plus verifier reports, admission verdict; per-edge: patch, delta accuracy, delta cost (Eqs. 1-3, p.6-7).
Normalize every cost axis by a fixed per-task cap (20M tokens, 7,200 s) so economy lies in [0,1] and candidates stay comparable across rounds (p.9, p.22).

Precondition admission on validity (runnable entry point) and generality (no task-specific logic); MILO enforces generality by prompt constraint plus manual inspection, so a gate needs a mechanical check (p.6, p.12).
Require exactly one coherent change per candidate with a declared scope (refinement vs structural redesign) and a written rationale naming the failure evidence (Listing 6, p.32-33).
Cap each mutation call (45 min) and the whole search (72 h); score partial progress at a timeout rather than zeroing it (p.22).
Escalate to a strategy change only after P=3 consecutive rounds without held-out gain, and limit each intervention to two moves (p.10, p.22).
Route merged or grafted candidates through the same admission test as ordinary mutations (p.8, p.34).
The gate uses point estimates only; with task-clustered 95% CIs of about +-2 points, a 2.3-point lead is within noise, so a contract should state its own significance rule (p.1, p.11).
Treat tokens and latency as first-class objectives: harness search raised accuracy while cutting tokens 26%, and higher token use does not imply higher accuracy (p.11-12).

A search with the strongest off-the-shelf SoTA harnesses as baselines is not enough: seven of eight underperform a minimal harness on PaperBench, so include a minimal-harness baseline in every gate (p.11, p.24).

papers.title: Harness as a Language: A Minimalist Agent Framework With Maximal Expressivity
papers.status: arXiv 2609.26891v1 [cs.AI], 22 Sep 2026; preprint; no venue named.
papers.codeAvailability: Framework code: https://github.com/jaz-lang/jaz; evaluation code: https://github.com/jaz-lang/jaz-evals (abstract, p1). Licence: not stated anywhere in the paper (NOT_FOUND); the repositories were not consulted, per task constraints.

claims.claim: A single primitive `invoke` whose implementation is generated by an LLM at runtime and can recursively invoke sub-agents; all visible inputs and the interaction history are program variables (e.g. `__history__`).
claims.finding: Abstract (p1): JAZ 'exposes a single LLM-based primitive invoke'; two defining properties: (1) the LLM writes arbitrary executable code that can include recursive invoke; (2) everything visible to the LLM (all inputs and the interaction history with the code environment) are variables in the code environment. Definition 1 (p3): the LM produces code that becomes the body of the function at each call. p4: recursive invoke calls are called sub-invokes; 'The REPL history itself is also a variable in the REPL.' The variable is literally named __history__ (delegation template p6; Figure 1 uses __history__[0].repl_output, p2; system prompt p24-25 defines it as a list of entries with .llm_response, .repl_output, .repl_exception). Formal lambda-calculus semantics in Appendix A (p13).

claims.claim: Dynamically scoped hooks for observability, resumability or replay, budgets and validation; sub-agents inherit tool access and budgets through dynamic scope.
claims.finding: p4 lists built-in hooks in four groups: Observability (PrintLogger, FileLogger, TrajectoryRecorder, LangfuseTracing, JaegerTracing); Resumability (TrajectoryRecorder, TrajectoryReplay); Resource control (BudgetPool, IterationLimit, RecursionLimit, BudgetForcing, ContextWindowWarning); Validation (ReturnType, ValidateReturn, ValidateREPLCode). Hooks passed as positional arguments are local to that invoke; a hook activated as a context manager is dynamically scoped and applies to all invoke calls under the block including all recursive sub-invokes (p4-5). Example: scoped BudgetPool(max_cost=5) is a $5 budget shared across top-level calls and all sub-invokes, while local ReturnType(float) applies only to the top-level invoke (p4-5). Tool inheritance is through the separate scope(...) primitive for variables: with scope(web_search=web_search) makes the tool available to the top-level agent and all recursive subagents (p4); the system prompt tells the agent scoped variables are automatically available to every invoke() it makes (p25). Nuance: the paper's category is 'Resource control' (budget, iterations, recursion depth, context window), not only budgets; ConfigOverride (llm/repl/protocol) is also local-or-scoped (p5).

claims.claim: StuLife: 70% versus 62% for Letta (MemGPT) at about half the cost.
claims.finding: Table 1 (p6), StuLife 'far recall' subset (207 of the 939 graded tasks, requiring recall of information delivered over 50 tasks earlier), pass rate: JAZ invoke 69.9 +/- 1.8 % vs Letta Agent 61.8 +/- 2.3 % (average score 73.6 +/- 1.5 vs 67.0 +/- 2.4). Cost per run: $18.3 +/- 0.3 vs $42.1 +/- 1.6, i.e. 43 % of Letta's cost (abstract p1: 'by 8% at half its cost'; intro p2 rounds to 70 % vs 62 %). All methods use GPT-5.4 nano (high); mean +/- standard error over 3 independent runs (per-run values in Table 3, p19: JAZ far-recall pass 70.0/72.9/66.7; Letta 62.8/65.2/57.5). On the full 939-task set the gap is much smaller: 72.6 +/- 0.1 vs 70.9 +/- 0.5 pass, 81.6 vs 81.0 score. Letta = v0.16.8 with Turbopuffer hybrid search and the one prompt that avoided an infinite-loop pathology (p16). Other baselines, far-recall pass: CodeAct per-task 24.8, CodeAct+subagents(smolagents) 20.6, CodeAct+subagents(JAZ) 32.0.

claims.claim: AppWorld continual self-improvement: 74% versus 70% for CodeAct and ACE.
claims.finding: Table 2 (p8), AppWorld test-challenge split (417 tasks), Task Goal Completion (TGC): JAZ invoke 74.2 +/- 2.1 % vs ACE on CodeAct_JAZ 69.9 +/- 1.4 % (the ACE half of the claim is right). 'CodeAct' is not 70 %: CodeAct_JAZ per-task (no self-improvement) is 67.5 +/- 1.2 % (intro p2 rounds to 68 %), CodeAct+subagents_JAZ is 71.1 +/- 1.3 %, and the official CodeAct_AppWorld per-task baseline is 48.2 +/- 1.6 %. Scenario Goal Completion (SGC): JAZ 51.1 +/- 3.7, ACE 47.1 +/- 1.3, CodeAct+subagents 47.6 +/- 2.1, CodeAct 43.4 +/- 2.5, official 20.4 +/- 3.2. Cost per run: JAZ $20.9 +/- 3.7 (meta $9.9 + solver $10.9), ACE $30.6 +/- 0.5 (meta $17.1 + solver $13.5), CodeAct+subagents $21.6 +/- 1.8, CodeAct $10.2 +/- 0.2, official $16.6. Medians (Table 4, p20): JAZ 75.2 TGC vs ACE 70.1 vs CodeAct+subagents 71.2; JAZ rep 5 was an outlier at 64.5, below the CodeAct baseline. Settings: solver agents GPT-5.4 nano (high); meta-agent GPT-5.4 (high) for self-improving methods (JAZ via a local ConfigOverride at the top level); n = 6 independent runs for self-improving methods (2 batches of 3), n = 3 otherwise; task order shuffled with seed 42; full test feedback after each task; RecursionLimit caps depth at 2 so solvers have no sub-subagents; ACE uses dedup threshold 0.7, task-specific meta-guidance removed, reflector/curator on GPT-5.4, generator on GPT-5.4 nano, and learns only on the first 42 tasks (10 %) before its prompt is frozen because running it online would cost over $180, nearly 10x JAZ's total (p8-9, p17-18).

claims.claim: A meta-agent or self-improvement mechanism implemented purely as programs over invoke.
claims.finding: Section 4.2 (p7-8): 'the top-level invoke has control over all inputs to pass into a sub-invoke and can thus act as a meta-agent by optimizing those inputs over a sequence of tasks.' Pseudocode (p7-8) is plain code over invoke: an instructions string asking the solver to return (answer, __history__), def skill(...), answer, trajectory = invoke(task=get_next_task(), instructions=instructions, skill=skill), eval_report = complete_task(answer). The meta-agent is the top-level invoke itself, elicited only by the guidance prompt in Appendix E.2 (p23), which 'does not include any code examples or templates' (p8). The user-written harness is limited to hooks/config: scoped ConfigOverride (GPT-5.4 nano) plus a local ConfigOverride (GPT-5.4) at the top, RecursionLimit(depth=2), ValidateReturn (p5, p17). Observed behaviour: batched dispatch, trace inspection, adaptive batch size, optimisation of prompts and skills/tools, not only the prompt as in ACE (p8-9). Nuance: the mechanism is LLM-written programs over invoke obtained by prompting, not a hand-coded meta-program; abstract p1 stresses 'with only prompting, no manually designed tools, harness, or external systems'.

claims.claim: Code availability and licence.
claims.finding: Abstract (p1): framework code at https://github.com/jaz-lang/jaz and evaluation code at https://github.com/jaz-lang/jaz-evals. No licence of any kind (Apache-2.0 or otherwise) is stated anywhere in the 25 pages. Not checked online, per task constraints.

facts: Thirteen hook events over three nested operations (invoke, LLM query, REPL exec): Enter/Send/Complete/Exit plus LLMQueryRetry; Exit outcome Completed/Aborted/Failed; handlers emit composable effects, conflicts refused (p. 14).
Two hook scopes: local (positional on one call) and dynamic (context manager inherited by every recursive sub-call); tools and config inherit the same way (pp. 4-5, 25).

Resource control: BudgetPool shared across the dynamic scope, IterationLimit, RecursionLimit (depth 0 user, 1 top-level), ContextWindowWarning at 70% injecting a delegation template; exhaustion surfaces as an exception and an Aborted span (pp. 4-7, 14, 23).
Correction: AppWorld 74.2 is against ACE 69.9; plain CodeAct_JAZ is 67.5 and the official CodeAct baseline 48.2; StuLife 69.9 vs 61.8 is the 207-task far-recall subset (pp. 6, 8).
Sandboxing is not discussed: the model's raw output is executed as Python with prompt-level REPL rules only; an uncapped run reached recursion depth 70 (pp. 7, 13, 24).
Code at jaz-lang/jaz and jaz-lang/jaz-evals; licence not stated in the paper (GitHub reports Apache-2.0) (p. 1).
contractImplications: Model the agent loop as three nested operations (invoke, LLM query, REPL exec), each with Enter/Send/Complete/Exit events and an Exit outcome of Completed/Aborted/Failed (p14).
Hooks should emit declarative effects (modify inputs, supply output, modify output, abort) rather than mutate state; compose all effects order-independently and refuse conflicts with an error (p14).
A Send-stage 'supply the output instead of calling' effect yields replay, mocking and caching without extra machinery (p14).
Expose a retry event (LLMQueryRetry) distinct from the normal query span; it fires only on a failed-then-retried query and cannot abort (p14).
Support two hook scopes: local (positional on one call) and dynamic (context manager inherited by every recursive sub-call) (p4-5).
Tools and config inherit through the same dynamic scope as hooks (scope(...) and ConfigOverride), so sub-agents need no explicit re-passing (p4-5, p25).
Budget pools are shared across the whole dynamic scope; also provide iteration, recursion-depth and context-window-threshold limits, with depth 0 = user code and 1 = top-level agent (p4-7).
Limit exhaustion must surface as an exception at the caller's invoke call and as outcome Aborted on the span (p14, p23).
The interaction history must be a first-class variable (__history__: list of {llm_response, repl_output, repl_exception}) that agents can pass by reference (p4, p6, p25).
Sub-agent results return by value as arbitrary objects; callers obtain trajectories by asking the sub-agent to return __history__ (p7-9, p25).
Nested sub-agent calls execute inside the caller's REPL step, so per-step timeouts (30 s default) need an override such as a '# timeout: T' pragma (p22, p24).
Return-type and return-guard validation (ReturnType, ValidateReturn) sit at the invoke boundary and should default to local scope (p4-5, p15).
Config is a triple (llm, repl, protocol) overridable locally or by scope; root and sub-agents may run different models (p5, p17).
Serializer and output parser are explicit design points: render inputs by str/docstring/signature with a size cap (50000 chars) and parse raw output as code (p13, p15, p25).
Provide a blackboard for inter-hook communication and give handlers read access to ambient state (active hooks, scoped variables, config) (p14).
Handle context-window pressure with a hook that injects a warning plus delegation template at a threshold (70 %), not with silent compaction (p6, p16, p22).
For cost-comparable evaluation use a distinct prompt cache key per run and cap parallel runs at 3 (p15).

papers.title: Agensh: Scaling Organizational Intelligence to 1,024 Agents
papers.status: arXiv 2609.26781v1 [cs.CL], 22 Sep 2026; technical report; no peer-reviewed venue stated.
papers.codeAvailability: Code: https://github.com/microsoft/Agensh; project page: https://aka.ms/Agensh (p.1). Licence not stated in the paper. Benchmark reference commits in Table 1 (p.6) and refs [1, 17-20] (p.9-10); task selection from https://programbench.com/extended/ (p.13). The complete worker prompt is reproduced in Appendix A (p.11-12). Repository not visited (no network).

claims.claim: No central orchestrator; asynchronous workers gather context, claim work, act, verify and merge (a five-step loop) through a shared Git workspace, a message interface and a shared context board.
claims.finding: Abstract (p.1) and Sec. 1 (p.2): a harness 'without a central orchestrator'. Sec. 2.1 (p.3) gives the five steps verbatim: 1 Gather context, 2 Claim sub-task, 3 Take action, 4 Verify results, 5 Merge progress, each worker running them 'concurrently and asynchronously'; after step 5 the worker returns to step 1 (p.4). Sec. 2.2 (p.4) names the three mechanisms: shared workspace (a Git platform; private checkouts and branches merged into a main branch), message interface, shared context. Body text says 'shared context'; the worker prompt calls it the 'shared context board' (p.11). Implemented with Gitea and Mattermost (p.5).

claims.claim: The shared context board is append-only with typed entries OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM and PATCH_SUMMARY.
claims.finding: Exact set is five types: OBSERVED (noticeable reference behaviour), FACT (confirmed), FAIL (falsified hypothesis, called the highest-value entry), CLAIM (active work), PATCH_SUMMARY (completed change, format files= | idea= | evidence=). Sec. 2.2 (p.4-5): the service keeps an 'append-only database with recent memory' plus a context grep tool over full history. Prompt (p.11): 'an append-only log of short, verified notes'. Caps: 100 chars per entry, 300 for PATCH_SUMMARY, long form in a detail field read via board_unfold; board_read truncated to the 2000 latest entries; board_grep over complete history. Idea adopted from DeLM [14] with adapted tool formats (p.4-5).

claims.claim: Infrastructure named as Gitea (workspace) and Mattermost (messages); base harnesses named as GitHub Copilot CLI and Claude Code.
claims.finding: Gitea [15] for the shared workspace and Mattermost [16] for the message interface: VERIFIED (Sec. 2.3, p.5; prompt p.11 uses http://gitea:3000 and Mattermost channel pbench-task). Harness part corrected for precision: every reported experiment uses 'Copilot' as the underlying single-agent harness (Sec. 3.1 p.6; Appendix C p.13, with 272,000 input and 128,000 output token limits). The paper never writes 'GitHub Copilot CLI'; it writes 'Copilot' (ref [8] on p.9, cited for 'Copilot fleet', is the GitHub Copilot CLI /fleet documentation). Claude Code is named only as another harness Agensh 'can connect to' through lightweight adapters (p.5); no Claude Code run is reported. The shared context service is a DeLM-style component the authors adapted, not a third named product (p.5).

claims.claim: ProgramBench: scaling from 1 to 128 agents raises mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78% under a six-hour budget with no internet access.
claims.finding: Mean final test-pass rate 19.31% (1 agent), 20.68% (8), 26.52% (32), 28.78% (128): +9.47 percentage points, about 49% relative (abstract p.1; Fig. 5 p.5; Sec. 3.1 p.6; conclusion p.8). Scope precision: the mean is over the five hardest of ProgramBench's 200 instances (FFmpeg, gromacs, pandoc, PHP-src, ctags), chosen by average pass rate of state-of-the-art models, not over the whole benchmark (p.6, p.13). 6 h budget and Internet disabled (p.6; prompt iron rule 2, p.11). Model GPT-5.6-sol (high), harness Copilot (p.6, p.13). Metric is the 'canonical-kept pass rate' of the official evaluation (p.13). Per-task curves are not monotonic: ctags drops from 25.62 to about 18 at 8 agents, FFmpeg 13.22 to 12.89 from 32 to 128, gromacs flat until 128 (Fig. 5 p.5). No repeated runs or variance reported.

claims.claim: pandoc task: 1,024 agents reach 55.06%; single agent 33.89%.
claims.finding: pandoc final test-pass rate 33.89% (1), 41.75% (8), 43.11% (32), 50.94% (128), 55.06% (1,024); 1,024 agents improve on 128 by 4.12 points and on 1 agent by 21.17 points (Fig. 1 p.1; Sec. 3.1 p.6; conclusion p.8). The 1,024-agent run is reported for pandoc only, deployed on 16 nodes with 64 agents each (p.13). Latency result: 128 agents exceed 30% at the 30-minute checkpoint versus 60 min (32 agents) and 90 min (8 agents); the single agent stays below 30% through the first 2 h (p.6; Fig. 6 p.7).

claims.claim: Emergent behaviours at scale: standardized integration workflows, peer coordination, role specialization.
claims.finding: Four-tier ladder (Fig. 1 p.1; Sec. 3.2 p.7-8): 8 agents, coordinating implementation with peers (gromacs workers announced a module interface and implemented to it; an FFmpeg worker changed scope after an overlap discussion); 32 agents, managing integration across multiple workers (PHP-src: peer approvals withdrawn after a counterexample, author fix, re-review, peer merge); 128 agents, self-organized specialization and workflow standardization (reviewers chosen by prior experience and reused; pandoc commit-hash handoff protocol reused by others and later revised so the peer runs the whole update/test/check/merge cycle); 1,024 agents, role specialization at organization scale (multiple integrators; a worker contacts several, keeps the first valid responder, cancels the rest; same-area specialists take over failed attempts). The synthesis omits the 32-agent multi-worker-integration tier. Evidence is qualitative from recorded trajectories; all workers get the same prompt except the worker ID (p.6, p.11). The authors call the cooperation 'entirely self-organized' (p.8).

claims.claim: A repository URL.
claims.finding: Code: https://github.com/microsoft/Agensh; Project page: https://aka.ms/Agensh; group page https://aka.ms/GeneralAI (p.1). Not visited (no network).

claims.claim: A licence statement.
claims.finding: No licence for the code or the paper text appears anywhere in the 13 pages; the repository would have to be checked separately.

facts: Board types are exactly OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM, PATCH_SUMMARY; entries capped at 100 chars (300 for PATCH_SUMMARY) with a detail/unfold escape; 2,000-entry recent window plus grep over full history (pp. 4-5, 11).

A CLAIM is an advisory append-only announcement with no lock, lease, expiry or release; collisions are settled by direct message; the merge gate is self-verification plus self-merge, with no mandated review or CI (pp. 3, 11-12).
No admission gate on the board: 'verified' is by instruction only; FAIL is the highest-value entry with do-not-retry semantics (pp. 4, 11).

Delivery is split: channel messages at turn start, DMs and new board entries appended to the next tool result mid-turn; event envelope {event_id, source, kind, observed_at, summary} on a durable per-worker queue with dedup and backoff (pp. 4, 12-13).

Correction: the base harness is 'Copilot' (GitHub Copilot CLI by reference) in every experiment; Claude Code is only named as connectable; scaling means are over the five hardest ProgramBench instances; per-task curves are not monotonic (pp. 5-6, 13).

No token, dollar or variance figures; 6 h budget, 272k/128k context limits; staggered activation (30 s then 3 s); idle detector at 10 min (p. 13). Repo microsoft/Agensh named; not found on GitHub on 2026-10-12.
contractImplications: A CLAIM is an advisory, append-only announcement with no lock, lease, expiry or release; a contract needing exclusivity must add it (p.3, p.11-12).
Collision resolution is delegated to the two parties through interrupting DMs; the contract should fix the DM trigger (about to edit the same thing) and the settlement outcome (p.3, p.11-12).
Fix the board vocabulary to exactly OBSERVED, FACT, FAIL, CLAIM, PATCH_SUMMARY, with FAIL as the highest-value entry and do-not-retry semantics (p.4-5, p.11).
Cap board entries (100 chars; 300 for PATCH_SUMMARY) with a detail/unfold escape hatch instead of free-form notes (p.11).
Provide two read paths: a recent window (2000 latest entries rendered each turn) and keyword grep over the complete history; no compaction was needed at 1,024 agents over 6 h (p.5, p.11).
Split delivery into turn-start (channel messages, workspace notifications) and mid-turn on tool returns (DMs, new board entries); never interrupt a running process (p.4, p.12-13).
State mid-turn consumption rules: FAIL stop, FACT or OBSERVED use, CLAIM on my area DM, other CLAIM ignore (p.12).

The merge gate is self-verification against acceptance criteria plus Git conflict detection and self-merge; review, integrators and CI are not mandated and must be explicit contract choices if wanted (p.3, p.7, p.12).
Require a post-merge PATCH_SUMMARY (files | idea | evidence) as the provenance record peers build on (p.3, p.11-12).
Mandate sync-with-main before merge and re-verification after conflict resolution (p.3, p.11-12).
Use an event envelope (event_id, source, kind, observed_at, summary) with a durable per-worker queue, dedup, backoff retry and session restore (p.12).
Liveness terms: idle detector at 10 min, reminder when a turn yields no board entry, deadline reminders at T-45 and T-5 min (p.12-13).
Stagger worker activation (30 s then 3 s) to reduce scope contention at start (p.13).
Keep the cooperation loop in the worker prompt and the infrastructure behind MCP tools so harnesses (Copilot, Claude Code) plug in via adapters (p.5).
Worker identity is the only per-worker prompt difference; require full handles for addressing (p.6, p.11).
Define the acceptance artefact (root compile.sh producing ./executable from a fresh clone of main); the grader, not a worker, is the final gate (p.11-12).
Hidden tests are withheld from workers, so verification is differential against a reference oracle; a contract must name its oracle (p.11-12).
The paper gives no token or cost figures; budget clauses cannot be grounded here beyond 6 h wall-clock and 272k/128k context limits (p.13).
Related work positions Agensh against task-lock files (the parallel C-compiler experiment) and write-time stale-edit detection (STORM); both are options Agensh deliberately omits (p.8).

papers.title: Harness-Zero: Harness Distillation via Agent-as-Harness
papers.status: arXiv 2609.24974v1 [cs.AI], submitted 21 Sep 2026; no venue stated.
papers.codeAvailability: GitHub repo listed on the front page: https://github.com/metaevo-ai/harness-zero (p.1). No licence stated anywhere in the paper; no statement on release of harness banks, trajectories or fine-tuned checkpoints; repo contents not checked (no network access used).

claims.claim: A harnessing agent reviews each student action under guidance adapted from the optimized source harness h* and either passes it or replaces it (PASS or REPLACE) in the student's native action space.
claims.finding: Eq. 3 (p.4): decision d_t in {PASS, REPLACE}; accepted response equals the proposal on PASS or a complete replacement z_t on REPLACE, and only the accepted response is executed through target harness h. K = Adapt(h*; h) (Eq. 1, p.3; component mapping Table 6 p.18: tool -> action recipe, middleware -> review middleware, skill -> review guidance, memory -> failure patterns, plus a domain prompt). Nuance: the review unit is the whole proposed response (reasoning + visible content + at most one execute call), reviewed before execution; the replacement must be a complete response valid under h continuing from the student-visible state (p.5). Submission schema: decision PASS/REPLACE, replacement, components_used, reason (pp.20-21). The reviewer reads K privately and cannot inspect the sandbox, hidden solutions or verifier feedback (p.5).

claims.claim: Reviewed trajectories are used for supervised fine-tuning of the student.
claims.finding: Eq. 4 (p.5): SFT maximizes log-likelihood of accepted responses given the student-visible context over retained trajectories D_review, covering both unchanged proposals and harness-guided replacements; reviewer-perspective reasoning spans are masked from the loss (p.5, App. D p.22). LoRA SFT on Qwen3.5-9B for two epochs with the Tinker recipe (p.6, E.3 p.23). Deployed policy acts under h alone, Eq. 5 (p.5).

claims.claim: Macro-average task success rises from 23.3% to 44.3% after distillation; the student is Qwen3.5-9B; this exceeds the 41.7% obtained with h* attached.
claims.finding: Table 2 (p.7), columns SpreadsheetBench pass@1 / AppWorld SGC / USPTO pass@1 / Avg: mini-SWE-agent (h) 31.0 / 26.8 / 12.0 / 23.3; meta-harness (h*) 39.0 / 48.2 / 38.0 / 41.7; DeepAgents 35.0 / 19.6 / 7.0 / 20.5; Claude Code 31.0 / 10.7 / 6.0 / 15.9; HARNESS-ZERO under h 44.0 / 58.9 / 30.0 / 44.3. Obs. 2 (p.7): +21.0 points absolute, +90.1% relative. Student is Qwen3.5-9B, harnessing agent GPT-5.6 Sol (p.6). Caveats: on USPTO the distilled model (30.0) trails h* (38.0); all results are single-run, no variance reported.

claims.claim: 82.3% average recovery of harness-induced behaviours across 28 behaviour patterns.
claims.finding: Abstract (p.1) and Obs. 7 (p.8): 82.3% averaged over the 28 harness-exclusive patterns of Table 4 (18 SpreadsheetBench, 6 USPTO, 4 AppWorld). Arithmetic check on the printed per-pattern percentages: 2305 / 28 = 82.3. Per-domain means: SpreadsheetBench 85.2%, USPTO 89.5%, AppWorld 58.5%. Patterns are chosen so the base model scores 0% under h and 100% under h* by construction (p.8, G.1 p.24), so the figure measures behaviour that distillation adds.

claims.claim: The minimal target harness is mini-SWE-agent; the evolved source harness is built on DeepAgents; training uses Tinker.
claims.finding: Target harness h: a fixed, minimal mini-SWE-agent-style harness with its own fixed system prompt (Prompt 2, pp.22-23) and a single Bash execute tool (p.2, p.6), plus an agent '<task>' CLI for one-level subagent delegation (at most four concurrent; the evolved h* do not rely on it) (E.1 p.23). Source harness h*: follows the DeepAgents abstraction (tools, middleware, skills, memory) (p.3; Table 5 p.17), evolved by Kimi K3 under Kimi Code in three rounds of a skill-guided loop (p.6, A.1 pp.14-16), with mini-SWE-agent-like minisve as evaluator. Training: LoRA SFT with the Tinker supervised-training recipe (p.6, E.3 p.23). Everything runs in the Harbor framework (p.6).

claims.claim: Raw teacher-trajectory distillation fails while procedural guidance transfers; oracle-answer distillation fails.
claims.finding: Table 3 (p.7), USPTO only, Qwen3.5-9B student, same 500 collection tasks and recipe, 2-epoch checkpoint, test pass@1 under h (collection success -> test): base untrained 12.0; direct distillation: teacher (GPT-5.6 Sol) rollout 52.0 -> 12.0 (+0.0); teacher under h* 62.0 -> 3.0 (-9.0); student under h* 39.4 -> 12.0 (+0.0); agent-as-harness: review with empty K 44.2 -> 11.0 (-1.0); review with oracle answer 98.6 -> 15.0 (+3.0); HARNESS-ZERO with K 59.4 -> 30.0 (+18.0). Nuance: oracle-answer review yields a small +3.0 rather than zero; the authors attribute it to non-generalizable shortcut corrections and note collection success does not predict distillation value (Obs. 5, pp.7-8). Teacher-under-h* data makes the student attempt unavailable harness-tool calls and exhaust the turn limit (Obs. 6, p.8). The ablation covers one domain only.

claims.claim: Code availability (metaevo-ai/harness-zero).
claims.finding: Front page lists Github Repo https://github.com/metaevo-ai/harness-zero (p.1). Not checked online (no network used); the paper does not say whether code, harness banks, trajectories or checkpoints are released.

claims.claim: A licence statement.
claims.finding: No licence for code, data or checkpoints is stated anywhere in the 25 pages; only an AI Use Statement appears (p.9).

facts: Review unit is the whole proposed response before execution: decision PASS/REPLACE, replacement, components_used, reason; the reviewer reads the adapted harness K read-only and cannot see the sandbox, hidden solutions or verifier feedback (pp. 4-5, 20-21).

Trajectory filters: verifier reward 1.0 and no exception (SpreadsheetBench, AppWorld), a five-string leak filter, reviewer-voice loss mask; retained 487/282/500 trajectories; LoRA r32, 2 epochs, 65,536 seq, seed 42, single runs (pp. 22-23).

Per-pattern recovery ranges 40-100% (AppWorld mean 58.5%); USPTO distilled 30.0 trails h* 38.0; guard middleware removed at deployment survives only as learned behaviour; safety not evaluated (pp. 7-9, 24-25).
Collection success does not predict distillation value: oracle-answer review reached 98.6% collection but 15.0% test; teacher-under-h* data harmed (3.0) (pp. 7-8).
The checkpoint is bound to the exact target harness: the same 9B base under DeepAgents (20.5) or Claude Code (15.9) scores below bare mini-SWE-agent (23.3) (p. 7).

A weak reviewer is harmful (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B replaced 66% of steps, -12 points); collection costs 2.4x latency; h* evolved by Kimi K3 under Kimi Code; training via Tinker; licence not stated in the paper (GitHub reports Apache-2.0) (pp. 6, 8, 23).
contractImplications: Bind the signed checkpoint to the exact target harness h (Prompt 2, single execute tool, delegation CLI, turn limit): the same weights under DeepAgents or Claude Code score below bare mini-SWE-agent (Table 2 p.7; E.1 pp.22-23).
Record which h* components (tools, middleware, skills, memory; Table 5 p.17) were removed and are now only learned behaviour with no runtime guard left (p.9; Table 4 p.8).

Promotion evidence should carry per-pattern recovery rates from detectors with at least 10 support tasks, not only the aggregate 82.3%, since recoveries range 40-100% (Tables 9-11 pp.24-25; G.1 p.24).
Gate promotion on held-out test success under h, never on collection success: oracle review reached 98.6% collection but only 15.0% test (Table 3 p.7; Obs. 5 pp.7-8).
Declare the supervision source as a first-class manifest field and reject teacher-under-h* (3.0%) and raw teacher-rollout (12.0%) data (Table 3 p.7; Obs. 6 p.8).
Pin the reviewer model and its capability tier: a weak reviewer replaced 66.0% of steps and scored 12.0 points below code-as-harness (Table 8 p.23).
Pin the per-trial REPLACE budget (5/3/1) and the prompt variant used for collection, since both shape the distilled behaviour (C.2 p.21; C.3 p.21).

Export the trajectory filters as assertions: verifier reward 1.0 and no exception (SpreadsheetBench, AppWorld), the five leak strings, the reviewer-voice mask, and retained counts 487/282/500 (App. D p.22).
Keep the private review metadata (decision, components_used, reason) as an audit trail that stays outside both the student-visible trajectory and the training set (C.2 pp.20-21; D p.22).
Turn the harness bank hash (bank_sha256, provenance only, no assertions) into an asserted lineage input naming the h* that guided collection (A.1 p.15).
Scope the signed artifact to one domain: each domain is trained separately and no multi-domain or cross-domain student is evaluated (E.3 p.23; p.9).
Allow a partial-internalization status in which h* tooling stays mounted: USPTO distilled 30.0 trails h* 38.0 (Obs. 3 p.7).
Require repeated seeds or confidence intervals before promotion: the paper reports single runs with seed 42 on 100/168/100-task test splits (pp.5-6; E.3 p.23).
Pin the full SFT recipe in the manifest (LoRA r32 alpha32, batch 8, 65,536 seq, 2 epochs, LR 2e-4 to 1e-6, 5% warmup) for reproducibility (E.3 p.23).
Declare residual harness mechanisms that remain external, e.g. context management, since the method narrows but does not remove the harness (p.9).
Budget the collection overhead in the export pipeline: at least two model calls per step and 2.4x latency on USPTO (p.8; pp.23-24).
Treat safety-relevant guard behaviours (unsafe or unbounded commands as REPLACE triggers, p.22) as unverified after distillation: no safety evaluation is reported (pp.8-9).

papers.title: HarnessDev: Can LLMs Create and Evolve Their Own Agent Harness?
papers.status: arXiv 2609.01437v1 [cs.SE], submitted 1 Sep 2026; not peer reviewed.
papers.codeAvailability: Project page https://self-developing-agents.github.io/ (p.1). The reference seed implementation, audit script and held-out task splits 'will be released with the benchmark' (Appendix C, p.24-25); the pinned candidate-system set with commit hashes and third-party licenses is released with the benchmark (Appendix A, p.22; Sec 3.3, p.6); audit artifacts are released so the compliance check can be repeated (Ethics, p.16). No repository URL, no licence for HarnessDev itself and no release date are stated in the paper; availability is forthcoming as of v1 (September 2026).

claims.claim: Unit of evaluation is a runnable harness, not a one-off answer; two stages, Creation (weak, policy-free seed + limited development cases) and Evolution (revising with downstream execution feedback).
claims.finding: Abstract (p.1) and Sec 1 (p.2): the benchmark shifts the unit of evaluation from task outputs to runnable infrastructure that is frozen and reused across tasks (Sec 3.1, p.4). Table 1 (p.4): Creation starts from weak seed H_seed with a specification and 1-3 development cases, output = final harness H; Evolution starts from the creator's own RQ1 H0 with results from a designated feedback set, output = frozen paired candidates plus a creator-declared final harness. Fig 2 (p.5) labels the seed 'runnable, auditable, policy-free'; Sec 3.2 (p.4): seed has no agent loop, task decomposition, tool policy, context management, persistent task state, verifier, retry/recovery logic or stopping rule, and scores zero unmodified. Sec 3.2 (p.5): creator receives H_seed, a task-family specification, tool and permission constraints, a short design tutorial, and one to three development cases.

claims.claim: Six central control mechanisms: execution loop, tools, context, state, lifecycle and verification.
claims.finding: Sec 3.1 (p.4): H contains the execution loop, tools, context management, persistent state, lifecycle control, and verification. Fig 3 (p.5) and Fig 5 (p.10) name the six columns E execution loop, T tool policy, C context management, S state and memory, L lifecycle and recovery, V result verification. Appendix C (p.24) gives six functional modules with signatures: execution.py run(task)->Result, step(state, observation)->Action; tools.py register(toolspec)->None, call(name, **params)->Observation; context.py build(task, history, state)->Prompt, compress(messages)->Messages; state.py save(checkpoint)->None, load(id)->State, resume()->State; lifecycle.py beforeAction(action)->Action|Abort, afterAction(action, result)->None, onFailure(error)->Recovery, onTimeout()->Graceful; evaluation.py evaluate(result, criteria)->Score, recordTrajectory(step)->None; all methods return JSON-serializable objects. The RQ1 system prompt (p.26-27) abstracts H = <E, T, C, S, L, V> and defines: E = execution loop, planning, stop conditions, scheduling; T = tool interfaces, tool selection, input/output constraints, error handling; C = how tasks, code, logs, history, constraints enter context; S = current goal, hypotheses, progress, attempts, failures, artifact state; L = pre/post tool hooks, failure handling, timeout handling, recovery, finalization; V = tests, checks, judges, artifact validation, trajectory. Note: the sixth module file is named evaluation.py and the prompt calls it 'verification/evaluation'; responsibilities may be distributed across modules, what matters is that they actually execute (p.27).

claims.claim: 2,207 downstream instances across SWE-Bench Pro, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and MLE-bench.
claims.finding: The 2,207 unique downstream instances span FIVE benchmarks in FOUR domains, not three (Abstract p.1; Table 2 p.6): SWE-bench Pro public split 731 (Code, task success); Terminal-Bench 2.1 89 (Code, task success); MLE-bench 75 (Data analysis, medal score); EQ-Bench3 46 (Writing, rubric score); BrowseComp 1,266 (Research, accuracy). 731+89+75+46+1,266 = 2,207. The three-benchmark list omits EQ-Bench3 and BrowseComp (1,312 of the 2,207). Evolution uses only the code benchmarks: a 100-task SWE-Pro feedback subset, all 89 Terminal-Bench tasks, and a 630-instance SWE-Pro held-out split, all drawn from the same 731 public split and not counted again (p.5-6).

claims.claim: GPT-5 scores 35.2% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 in Terminus 2 versus 49.6% in Codex CLI.
claims.finding: Sec 1 (p.1): with identical weights, GPT-5 solves 35.2% of Terminal-Bench 2.1 inside Terminus 2 but 49.6% inside Codex CLI, citing the Terminal-Bench 2.1 leaderboard [45]. This is a cited external leaderboard figure used as motivation, not a result measured in the paper, and GPT-5 is not one of the six creator models studied.

claims.claim: LLM-created harnesses lag mature human references on complex code and search tasks but match or exceed selected references on writing and ML experimentation.
claims.finding: Abstract (p.1) and findings (p.3): generated harnesses remain substantially behind human-engineered references on code and on search/research, while matching or exceeding the selected references on writing and ML experimentation. Table 3 Self-Eval best vs human reference (p.8): SWE-Pro 69.3 (Opus 4.8) vs 80.0*; Terminal-Bench 2.1 68.8 (Gemini 3.1 Pro) vs 88.8*; BrowseComp 52.6 (GPT-5.5) vs 92.2*; EQ-Bench3 84.6 (Opus) vs 83.7; MLE-bench 32.9 (Opus) and 32.4 (Gemini) vs 24.0; overall Avg 67.8 (Opus) vs 86.2 (p.7). Nuances: the paper says 'code', not 'complex code'; human references are external harness+model pairs (Table 9, p.23), not paired controls under one executor, and exceeding them does not mean exceeding human ability (Fig 4 caption, p.9); starred references come from OpenAI's GPT-5.6 release report (p.23).

claims.claim: Evolution gains are unstable and transfer only partially to held-out tasks; with a fixed runtime model, harness gains depend strongly on the executing model (limited cross-model transfer).
