claims.finding: Abstract (p.1), Sec 4.3 (p.11) and Table 6 (p.12): all five self-runtime lineages improve on the visible feedback pair (+3.0 to +13.9 pair points) but held-out-630 gains shrink to +1.43..+4.44 (mean +3.11); under the fixed Gemini executor only Opus improves on held-out (+2.70) while Qwen (-1.11), DeepSeek (-2.38) and GPT-5.5 (-10.32) regress. Stability (p.13): of 64 official version switches, 8 regress on both benchmarks, 16 show a single-benchmark regression, 3 a cross-benchmark trade-off, 7 no measurable change, 27 gains inside the repeated-run noise band, 2 clear positive evidence, 1 no executable code change; the same commit varies by about +/-4.75 pair-score points; feedback and held-out scores move in the same direction only 34/64 times (53.1%); only 2/9 declared versions are held-out optimal. Cross-executor dependence in Creation (p.8, p.10): Opus SWE-Pro falls 69.3 -> 33.0 under Gemini, writing 84.6 -> 74.2; Qwen gains +17.6 on BrowseComp and +12.9 on MLE-bench under Gemini; an Opus harness hard-coding a 120-step limit nearly collapses under Gemini (p.7). Discussion (p.15): changing only the runtime binding can substantially move H0 and alter which harness changes are useful.

claims.claim: Substantial differences in execution token cost between harnesses not explained by task quality.
claims.finding: Findings (p.3): harnesses from different creators differ substantially in executor tokens consumed, and higher execution cost does not reliably produce better results. Sec 4.2 (p.8): MLE-bench token use varies about nineteen-fold (Table 3: 29.3M GPT-5.5 to 557.1M Seed 2.0 Pro) yet higher cost does not reliably produce a higher score. Fig 9 (p.23): GPT-5.5 reaches medal rate 19.1 with 29.3M tokens while DeepSeek V4 reaches 19.6 with 208.4M; BrowseComp DeepSeek 1,449.9M tokens for 40.9 vs Qwen 130.9M for 32.3 (Table 3). The paper's wording is 'does not reliably produce a higher score', slightly weaker than 'not explained by task quality'; the authors deliberately report the performance-token trade-off rather than a single cost-adjusted score (p.23).

claims.claim: Code or benchmark availability and licence.
claims.statusDetail: NOT_FOUND for licence and repository URL; release stated as forthcoming
claims.finding: Project page https://self-developing-agents.github.io/ (p.1). Appendix C (p.24-25): the reference seed implementation, the audit script and the held-out task splits 'will be released with the benchmark'. Appendix A (p.22) and Sec 3.3 (p.6): the pinned set of candidate harness systems with role assignments, commit hashes and licenses (of those third-party systems) is released with the benchmark. Ethics statement (p.16): built from public benchmark suites and open-source harnesses; audit artifacts released so the compliance check can be repeated; generated harnesses should be treated as untrusted code. No code repository URL, no licence for HarnessDev itself, and no release date are stated.

facts: Correction: 2,207 instances span five benchmarks in four domains (SWE-bench Pro 731, Terminal-Bench 2.1 89, MLE-bench 75, EQ-Bench3 46, BrowseComp 1,266); the 35.2% vs 49.6% GPT-5 figure is cited from the Terminal-Bench leaderboard, not measured (pp. 1, 6).

Six-module interface with signatures: execution run/step, tools register/call, context build/compress, state save/load/resume, lifecycle beforeAction/afterAction/onFailure/onTimeout, evaluation evaluate/recordTrajectory; honest tri-state status success/partial/failed (pp. 24, 27).

Score path isolated from the harness: self-reported status is never a scoring input; credit only from the real diff or final environment state; every run retains trajectory.jsonl, result.json and metrics beside frozen source (pp. 6-7).

Evolution: of 64 version switches only 2 are clear positives, 27 sit inside the ±4.75 repeated-run noise band; feedback and held-out move together 53.1% of the time; 2 of 9 declared versions were held-out optimal; fixed-executor lineages regress up to -10.32 (pp. 12-13).
Executor tokens vary nineteen-fold (29.3M to 557.1M on MLE-bench) without buying score; report cost beside capability and use avg@3 independent builds (pp. 7-8, 23).

Declared-but-dead mechanisms earn no credit (124/587 writing features, 36 data mechanisms on dead paths; no checkpoint event in 26,679 trajectories); 441 degenerate submissions went undetected (pp. 8-9, 13).

Matched-budget evaluation of harness evolution is explicitly future work; generated harnesses are untrusted code; release forthcoming on the project page (self-developing-agents.github.io) (pp. 15-16, 24).
contractImplications: Record the executor model and evaluator alongside every score; a score is comparable only when both are fixed within the comparison (p.6).
Score a frozen commit, never a moving working tree; the artifact under evaluation is the frozen harness source plus its runtime (p.4, p.6, p.29).
Keep an official-version rule: a candidate is admissible only after every required evaluation leg of the same commit settles; partial legs, probes and stopped runs never count (p.5-6, p.29-30).
Separate visible feedback scores from held-out scores and withhold held-out from the developer; store both in the record because they agree in direction only 53.1% of the time (p.6, p.12-13).
Store a repeated-run noise band with each configuration (paper: about +/-4.75 pair points on 189 tasks); an admission gate must not accept gains inside the band as improvement (p.13).
Do not admit by max visible score: only 2/9 declared versions were held-out optimal; require corroborating held-out or repeated runs before promotion (p.13).
Report execution cost (executor tokens total and mean per task, developer tokens excluded) next to capability; a nineteen-fold cost spread bought no score (p.7-8, p.23).
Treat a single build as unrepresentative: evaluate n independent builds (paper uses avg@3) when the configuration is produced by a stochastic creator (p.7).
Isolate the score path from the harness: self-reported status is never a scoring input; credit comes only from the real diff or final environment state (p.7).
Retain trajectory, result and metric artifacts beside the frozen source for post-hoc audit, and audit constraint compliance after every run (p.7, p.16).
Require honest tri-state status (success / partial / failed) with evidence; empty artifacts and plans are not completions, and the seed exits 'partial' (p.25, p.27).
Record executor-coupled parameters (step caps, timeouts, stopping rules, tool protocol) because they break on executor change; a 120-step hard-code collapsed one harness (p.7, p.10).
Validate final artifacts, not just status: 441 of 2,325 executed data tasks produced degenerate submissions no harness detected (p.8).
Count a mechanism only if traces show it on the main path during a formal run; declared-but-dead code earns no credit (p.9-10, p.28).
Pin per-task resource limits in the record: 500 steps and 7,200 s per code task; MLE-bench 36,000 s split 34,200 s harness plus 1,800 s grader reserve (p.22, p.29).
Enforce a fixed evaluation budget (10 full pairs, 2 probes per round, no banking) and a liveness guard instead of a wall-clock budget (p.29-30).
Dedup evaluations by (commit, benchmark); a resubmission returns the existing evaluation id rather than spending budget (p.29).
Zero the version on any prohibited route (hard-coded task IDs or answers, verifier probing, artifact tampering) and keep the per-task audit that proves it (p.6, p.30-31).
Require a provider-neutral runtime interface via model config or env vars; a harness that substitutes its own LLM access path is non-compliant (p.6, p.27-28).
Treat generated harnesses as untrusted code and isolate execution more strictly than reproducibility containers (p.16).
Prefer small verified changes over volume: edit size does not predict improvement and deletion can help as much as addition (p.8, p.12).

papers.title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies
papers.codeAvailability: NOT_FOUND. The paper contains no code release, repository URL or licence statement. Printed reproducibility material: Algorithm 1 (p.7), construction rules (App. B.3 p.20), prompt templates following DSPy conventions (App. D pp.23-28), and discovered prompts (App. E pp.28-32).

claims.claim: Three stages: block-level prompt optimization, workflow topology optimization, workflow-level prompt optimization.
claims.finding: Abstract (p.1) names the three stages as 1) block-level (local) prompt optimization, 2) workflow topology optimization, 3) workflow-level (global) prompt optimization, each conditioned on the output of the previous stage. Figure 3 (p.5) and Algorithm 1 (p.7) label them 1PO 'Block-level Prompt Optimization', 2TO 'Workflow Topology Optimization' and 3PO 'Workflow-level Prompt Optimization'. The introduction (p.2) describes stage 1 as a prompt 'warm-up' per topology block and stage 2 as search 'in a pruned set of topology space'. Section 3 (pp.5-7) uses the same three headings.

claims.claim: Topology optimization uses rejection sampling over an influence-weighted (incremental influence) search space; building blocks include aggregate, reflect, debate, summarize and tool-use.
claims.finding: p.6 defines the incremental influence I_a = E(a_i*)/E(a_0*), the selection probability p_a = Softmax(I_a, t), and rejects dimension a_i when u > p_a with u ~ Uniform(0,1), then samples configurations under an agent budget N(a) < B; Algorithm 1 line 13 (p.7) calls this 'Reject sampling'. Figure 3 caption (p.5) says Stage 2 samples from 'an influence-weighted design space'; Setup (p.8): 10 topologies searched 'via rejection sampling'. Blocks: Figure 3 caption (p.5) lists exactly Aggregate, Reflect, Debate, Summarize and Tool-use. Nuance: Sec. 2.2 (pp.4-5) presents Summarize as the worked example of a fourth category 'Custom Agents', and Tool-use as a binary code-execute insertion N_T in {0,1}; Table 3 (p.19) names the tool-use block 'Execute' (Executor).

claims.claim: The prompt optimizer is MIPRO (or MIPROv2); the prompt-optimized single agent is a strong baseline.
claims.finding: MIPRO is the optimizer in Sec. 2.1 (p.4, joint instruction and 1-shot exemplar optimization) and in Setup (p.8), where MASS is described as plug-and-play with arbitrary prompt optimizers. Fig. 5 caption and the ablation text (p.9) call the single-agent APO baseline 'MIPROv2'; both names are used for the same optimizer. Strength of the single-agent baseline: Fig. 2 (p.3) shows prompt-optimized agents dominating self-consistency, self-refine and debate per token on MATH with Gemini 1.5 Pro, and p.4 notes agent-scaling methods 'saturate much earlier'; Fig. 5 (p.9): CoT 63.5 -> APO single agent 68.0 average over 8 tasks on Gemini 1.5 Pro; Table 9 (p.23, MATH, Flash): CoT 66.7, MASS+APE 73.3, MASS+DSPy 78.2, MASS+MIPRO 81.0.

claims.claim: Benchmarks include MATH, DROP, HotpotQA and LiveCodeBench, with the models used.
claims.finding: Eight tasks (Sec. 4 p.7; App. B.1 p.18): reasoning = MATH, DROP; long-context multi-hop = HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA (LongBench versions); coding = MBPP, HumanEval, LiveCodeBench 'test output prediction' subtask. Models: gemini-1.5-pro-002 and gemini-1.5-flash-002 for all main results (p.7); key findings re-validated on Claude 3.5 Sonnet (claude-3-5-sonnet@20240620; 6 tasks, standard HotpotQA because of context window; Table 4 p.20) and Mistral Nemo 12B (mistral-nemo-12b; 4 tasks; Table 5 p.21). Metrics (Table 1 caption p.8): accuracy for MATH and LCB, F1 for DROP/HotpotQA/MuSiQue/2WikiMQA, pass@1 for MBPP/HumanEval. The same backbone serves as evaluator and optimizer (p.8).

claims.claim: MASS outperforms manually designed multi-agent systems and prior automated designs.
claims.statusDetail: VERIFIED; the paper reports averages as absolute scores, and the deltas in the finding are computed from Table 1.
claims.finding: Table 1 (p.8, mean of 3 test runs). Gemini 1.5 Pro average: MASS 78.79 vs CoT 65.28, Self-Consistency 68.18, Self-Refine 66.90, Multi-Agent Debate 70.26, ADAS 69.72 (AFlow* partial, reference only) -> +13.5 over CoT, +10.6 over SC, +8.5 over Debate, +9.1 over ADAS. Gemini 1.5 Flash average: MASS 74.30 vs CoT 60.87, SC 63.50, Self-Refine 63.46, Debate 65.91, ADAS 64.75 -> +13.4 / +10.8 / +8.4 / +9.6. Text p.8: 78.8% and 74.3% on average on Pro and Flash. Claude 3.5 Sonnet (Table 4 p.20, 6 tasks): 72.43 vs CoT 60.21, SC 62.84, Self-Refine 56.86, Debate 43.36. Mistral Nemo (Table 5 p.21, 4 tasks): 55.9 vs CoT 40.4, SC 46.3, Self-Refine 40.9, Debate 46.9. Graph-optimization baseline GPTSwarm (Table 8 p.23, MATH+HumanEval): 88.2 vs 80.5 on Pro, 82.9 vs 67.0 on Flash. Caveats the synthesis should carry: the AFlow comparison is 'not completely fair' (Claude 3.5 Sonnet optimizer, Gemini executor; p.8, p.20), AFlow beats MASS on 2WikiMQA (76.51 vs 73.34, Pro) and is described as 'competitive' on 2WikiMQA and HumanEval (p.9); ADAS beats MASS on MuSiQue with Flash (48.81 vs 43.67). MASS wins on average, not on every task.

claims.claim: Which design dimensions matter: prompt quality and search-space design versus scaling the agent count.
claims.finding: Abstract (p.1): prompts together with topologies 'play critical roles' in effective MAS design. Intro (p.2): prompts 'frequently form an influential design component', and influential topologies 'only represent a small fraction' of the full space. Sec. 2.1 (p.4): standard agent-scaling approaches (SC, Reflect) 'saturate much earlier' than prompt optimization; stated principle: 'optimize agents locally before scaling their topology'. Sec. 2.2 (p.4), via the NAS analogy: search-space design 'can be equally, if not more, critical' than the search method. Fig. 4 (p.6): on HotpotQA only debate helps (+3%), summarize hurts (-2%); on LCB reflect -15%, executor +10%, so 'not all topologies have a positive influence'. Design principles (p.10): optimize individual agents before composing; compose influential topologies; model agent interdependence via workflow-level joint optimization. App. C.3 (p.22): training-free baselines such as SC@9 are 'already saturated' and further inference spend brings 'marginal gains'.

claims.claim: Venue ICLR 2026 and the arXiv version date.
claims.finding: Footnote p.1: published in the fourteenth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR 2026). arXiv stamp on p.1: 2502.02533v2 [cs.LG] 31 Jan 2026.

claims.claim: Code availability and licence.
claims.finding: No code URL, repository, release statement or licence appears in the 32 pages (title page, conclusion p.11, acknowledgment p.11, appendices A-E pp.18-32 checked). Reproducibility material is limited to Algorithm 1 (p.7), construction rules (App. B.3 p.20), prompt templates (App. D pp.23-28, following DSPy conventions) and the best prompts discovered (App. E pp.28-32).

facts: A topology is an integer vector over blocks Aggregate {1,3,5,7,9}, Reflect {0-4}, Debate {0-4}, Summarize {0-4}, Execute {0,1}, composed in the fixed order summarize, reflect, debate, aggregate, under an agent budget B (pp. 4-6, 19-20).

Incremental influence I = E(block*)/E(single-agent*) after block-level prompt optimization, softmax t=0.05, rejection sampling of 10 candidates evaluated 3 times on a 50-100 item validation split; negative-influence blocks exist (Reflect -15% on LiveCodeBench) (pp. 6-8, 18).
Stage contributions on Gemini 1.5 Pro: CoT 63.5, single-agent APO 68.0, block-level PO 74.2, topology 77.3, workflow-level PO 78.8; the last stage regresses on some tasks (p. 9, 21).
Nothing transfers across backbones without re-optimization; transferred templates severely degrade basic topologies; results on Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Mistral Nemo are re-runs (pp. 7, 20-21).

Training cost about USD 5 on MATH (24M input, 11M output tokens); per-query inference 6,645 input / 3,263 output tokens; MASS wins on average, not every task (ADAS wins MuSiQue on Flash, AFlow 2WikiMQA on Pro) (pp. 8, 22).
ICLR 2026, arXiv v2 31 Jan 2026; no code, repository or licence; Algorithm 1, construction rules and prompt templates are the only reproducibility material (pp. 1, 7, 20, 23-32).
contractImplications: Topology contract: encode a workflow as an integer vector over named block dimensions (Aggregate, Reflect, Debate, Summarize, Execute) composed in the fixed order [summarize, reflect, debate, aggregate], not as a free-form graph (Table 3 p.19; p.6; App. B.3 p.20).
Topology contract: carry a hard agent-count budget B and reject any candidate with N(a) >= B; the paper's comparisons cap agents at 10 (p.6; p.8).

Admission gate: a block enters the topology search only after block-level prompt optimization has recorded its validation score; Stage 1 is the warm-up that keeps the search in an effective space, and the w/o-PO ablation degrades results (p.6; Fig. 5 right p.9).

Admission gate: use incremental influence I = E(block*)/E(single-agent*) as the admission score and prune dimensions with I < 1; negative-influence blocks exist (Reflect -15% on LCB, Summarize -2% on HotpotQA, Fig. 4 p.6).

Optimization engine: rejection sampling with 10 candidates x 3 validation evaluations suffices in the pruned space and is embarrassingly parallel, unlike the sequential ADAS and AFlow loops (p.8; Fig. 6 p.9).
Optimization engine: expose the softmax temperature (t = 0.05 is near-greedy) and the per-agent MIPRO budget (3 demos, 10 instruction candidates, 10 rounds) as contract parameters (p.8).
Admission gate: select on a validation subset (50-100 items) and report on a held-out test subset (100-200) over 3 runs with std; never admit on validation score alone (p.8; Table 2 p.18).

Admission gate: the final workflow-level joint PO adds about 2% on average but regresses on some tasks (HumanEval, MuSiQue), so admit it only when validation improves and keep the 2TO design as fallback (Table 6 p.21; p.9).

Contract: bind an admitted topology and its prompts to a backbone id; nothing is transferred across models without re-optimization, and transferred templates can severely degrade basic topologies (p.20; Tables 4-5 pp.20-21).

Contract: record training tokens and per-query inference tokens per stage using C = C(1PO) + C(2TO) + C(3PO); MASS training cost of about USD 5 on MATH is comparable to ADAS/AFlow and its per-query cost (6645 in / 3263 out) is close to multi-agent debate (App. C.3 p.21; Table 7 p.22).
Optimization engine: keep the prompt optimizer pluggable and recorded; optimizer choice alone moves MATH on Flash from 73.3 (APE) to 81.0 (MIPRO) (Table 9 p.23).
Admission gate: compare per task, not on the average; ADAS wins MuSiQue on Flash and AFlow wins 2WikiMQA on Pro (Table 1 p.8).

Contract: seed task-family priors (debate for multi-hop, aggregation for reasoning, reflect + executor for coding) but still search, since best configurations differ within a family (App. C.2 p.21; Fig. 8 p.19).
Engine: no reference implementation or licence is published; any engine must be rebuilt from Algorithm 1 (p.7), the construction rules (p.20) and the prompt templates (App. D pp.23-28).
